blocks.text: A client does not just send requests and wait.
It also has to listen, at any moment, for a notification the server decides to send on its own.
Event handling is the client side machinery that catches these incoming notifications and routes each one to the right piece of logic.
1. What Counts as an Event Here

blocks.alt: What Counts as an Event Here
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440476809-791405998.png
In this lesson, an event simply means any notification a client receives.
A resource changed, a tool list updated, a progress update, all of these arrive the same way, as a notification with no id, and all of them need some handler ready to catch them.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Every event in this lesson is, underneath, just an ordinary notification, the vocabulary changes, the mechanism does not.

blocks.text: Thinking of them as events, rather than raw notifications, just helps frame the client side responsibility clearly.
2. Registering a Handler
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440476809-939264943.png
A client typically registers one function per notification type it cares about, before the session even starts sending real traffic.
Most official MCP client SDKs provide this on style registration method directly, sparing a developer from writing the dispatch logic by hand.
Registering handlers early, before any traffic starts, avoids the narrow window where an event could arrive with nothing listening for it yet.
3. Dispatching by Method Name
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440476810-299845393.png
Underneath, a client reads the method field of every incoming notification and looks up the matching handler.
If no handler was registered for that specific method, a well behaved client simply ignores it rather than crashing.
4. Handlers Should Be Quick
A notification handler runs while the client is still able to receive other messages.
A slow, blocking handler can delay processing of everything else arriving on the same connection, keeping handlers fast, or offloading heavy work elsewhere, keeps the whole session responsive.
Queuing heavier work onto a background task, rather than doing it inline inside the handler, is a common way to keep the dispatch loop fast.

blocks.title: A useful rule of thumb
blocks.content: If a handler needs to make a network call or touch a database, it almost certainly belongs off the main dispatch path.

blocks.text: 5. One Notification, Multiple Interested Parts
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440476810-881079598.png
Sometimes more than one part of a host application cares about the same event.
A resource change might need to refresh a UI list and also invalidate a cache, a client can support multiple handlers per event type rather than forcing everything into one function.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Handler","Purpose"],"rows":[["refresh_ui","Updates what the user sees"],["invalidate_cache","Keeps stored data from going stale"]]}

blocks.text: Neither handler needs to know the other exists, each simply reacts to the same event independently.
6. Unregistering a Handler
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440476810-317468045.png
A handler tied to a specific screen or task should be removed once that screen closes or the task finishes.
Leaving stale handlers registered indefinitely is a common source of subtle memory leaks in a long running host application.
A screen that opens and closes repeatedly, registering a new handler each time without ever removing the old one, is a classic way this leak happens.
7. Events During Session Shutdown
A notification can technically arrive right as a session is closing.
A defensively written handler checks whether the session is still active before acting on a very late event, rather than assuming the connection is always healthy.
A handler that assumes the connection is always open can throw a confusing error at exactly the wrong moment.
This defensive check costs almost nothing and avoids a rare but real class of shutdown related bugs.
8. Testing Event Handlers in Isolation
A handler function can usually be tested on its own, without a real server, simply by constructing a fake notification object and calling the handler directly.
This kind of test runs instantly and needs no real server, making it easy to cover many different notification shapes quickly.
Covering the full range of shapes a specific notification type can take gives real confidence the handler will behave correctly in production.
9. Logging Events for Debugging
Logging every incoming notification, alongside its method and params, gives a clear trail when trying to understand why a client behaved a certain way at a specific moment.

blocks.title: A practical habit
blocks.content: Include the method name and a short summary of params in every logged event, full payloads can be large and are rarely all needed at once.

blocks.text: 10. Events vs Polling
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440476810-968043003.png
Before event handling, a client wanting to know about a change had to repeatedly ask, is anything new yet, over and over.
Event driven notifications remove that wasted repeated checking, the server simply speaks up the moment something actually changes.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Wasted requests","Latency to notice a change"],"rows":[["Polling","Many, most find nothing new","Up to one poll interval"],["Event handling","None","Immediate"]]}

blocks.text: This difference becomes especially significant at scale, a thousand clients polling every few seconds adds real, unnecessary load compared to the same clients simply waiting for an event.
Notifications shift that responsibility to the side that actually knows when something changed.
11. Wildcard or Catch-All Handlers
Some clients also support a catch all handler, one that fires for every notification regardless of method.
This is useful for logging or debugging, seeing everything that arrives, without needing to register a separate handler for each possible method name.

blocks.title: A caution
blocks.content: A catch all handler is great for observability, it should still avoid doing real work, leave that to the specific handlers registered for each method.

blocks.text: 12. Handler Errors Should Not Crash the Client

blocks.alt: Handler Errors Should Not Crash the Client
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440476810-456731298.png
If one handler throws an exception, that failure should not take down the whole event dispatch loop.
Wrapping each handler call in its own error boundary keeps one broken handler from silently breaking every other one registered for different events.
This same isolation pattern is a small, general safety net worth applying anywhere untrusted or third party code runs inside a shared loop.
13. A Worked Example
Trace registering two handlers and watching them fire as different notifications arrive during one session.

code.content:
client.on("notifications/progress", lambda n: print("progress:", n["params"]["percent"]))
client.on("notifications/tools/list_changed", lambda n: print("tools changed, refetching"))
# both fire independently whenever their matching notification arrives

blocks.text: Notice each handler only fires for its own specific method, a progress update never accidentally triggers the tools changed handler.
Adding a third handler for a completely different method requires no changes to the two already registered.
14. Common Mistakes When Handling Events

items: Writing a slow, blocking handler that delays every other message on the same connection.
Forgetting to unregister a handler tied to a closed screen, leaking memory over a long session.
Crashing on an unrecognized notification method instead of quietly ignoring it.
Never logging incoming events, making a strange client behavior impossible to trace back to its cause.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is letting one throwing handler silently prevent every other registered handler from running for the rest of the session.
A sixth common mistake is registering the exact same handler twice by accident, causing it to run twice for every matching event.
Checking a handler is not already registered before adding it again is a simple guard against this.
15. Practice: Build a Tiny Event Dispatcher
Write a small dispatcher that stores handlers in a dictionary keyed by method name, and calls every matching handler when a notification arrives.
Extend your dispatcher to also support a catch all handler, one that receives every notification regardless of its specific method.
Confirm your dispatcher still calls every other registered handler correctly even after one deliberately raises an exception.
Key Takeaway
Event handling is the client side counterpart to server initiated notifications, dispatching each incoming event by method name to whichever handlers registered interest in it.

This lesson closes out the notification side of the Communication Protocol module, the final lesson, Protocol Versioning, looks at how the specification itself changes over time without breaking existing clients and servers.
The error isolation pattern from the newly added section is a small addition that prevents one careless handler from quietly breaking an entire session.
